1472	### 11.6 Guarantees
1473	
1474	- Identical source, configuration, directory state and toolchain produce
1475	  identical bytes. Instructions combined into one file have a stable order.
1476	- Frontmatter values are quoted and escaped for the target format.
1477	- A missing reference target is reported instead of emitting a broken link.
1478	- Unsupported metadata is reported instead of being claimed as enforced.
1479	- Generated files are tracked in `.piton/manifest.json`, so cleanup never
1480	  deletes files users wrote. Its `targets` records, for each target, the
1481	  documentation date the generated files were validated against.
1482	- Failures name the source anchor and property. Output stays inside its
1483	  configured boundaries.
1484	
1485	### 11.7 Open decisions
1486	
1487	`spec/scope/belay/Decisions.pi` lists what is not decided. Tooling should say
1488	it is unspecified rather than guess:
1489	
1490	- Placement of instructions outside `shapeRoot`.
1491	- The types of `tools`, `allowed-tools` and `model`, and their mapping per
1492	  adapter.
1493	- Naming: skill filename normalization, command name normalization before the
1494	  `x-` prefix, acronym splitting and collision handling.
1495	- Whether workflows stay compositions of the four constructs. Do not add a
1496	  `workflow` keyword just because examples describe agent processes.
1497	- How platform-specific adapter options are written.
1498	
1499	Do not present any of these as settled. If your work depends on one, raise it
1500	with the user.
1501	
1502	## 12. Package management
1503	
1504	Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
1505	packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
1506	the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
1507	compile time.
1508	
1509	- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
1510	  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
1511	  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
1512	  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
1513	  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
1514	  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
1515	  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
1516	  root and dependencies.
1517	- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
1518	  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
1519	  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
1520	  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
1521	- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
1522	  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
1523	  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
1524	  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
1525	  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
1526	  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
1527	  `unknown-pin`.
1528	- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
1529	  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
1530	  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
1531	- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
1532	  to the project, and each package declares its own.
1533	- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
1534	  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
1535	  shown.
1536	- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
1537	  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
1538	  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
1539	  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
1540	  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
1541	- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
1542	  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
1543	  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
1544	  error.
1545	- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
1546	  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
1547	  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
1548	- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
1549	  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
1550	  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
1551	  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).
1552	
1553	The commands:
1554	
1555	- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
1556	  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
1557	  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
1558	- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
1559	  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
1560	  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
1561	  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
1562	- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
1563	  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
1564	  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
1565	  it.
1566	- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
1567	  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
1568	  imports the package.
1569	
1570	## 13. CLI reference
1571	
1572	Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
1573	✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
1574	and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
1575	coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
1576	text and stdout carries the bare results.
1577	
1578	| Command | Behaviour |
1579	| --- | --- |
1580	| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
1581	| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
1582	| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
1583	| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
1584	| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1585	| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
1586	| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
1587	| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1588	| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
1589	| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
1590	| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
1591	| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
1592	| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
1593	| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |
1594	
1595	Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
1596	(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
1597	and `namedArguments`.
1598	
1599	## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript
1600	
1601	`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:
1602	
1603	- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
1604	  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
1605	  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
1606	  whole specbase.
1607	- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
1608	  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
1609	  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
1610	- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
1611	  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
1612	  folding and selection ranges.
1613	- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
1614	  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
1615	  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
1616	  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
1617	- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
1618	  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
1619	  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
1620	- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
1621	- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
1622	  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
1623	  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.
1624	
1625	There is no signature help.
1626	
1627	Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
1628	empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
1629	after a `.` inside a string.
1630	
1631	Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
1632	extension:
1633	
1634	- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
1635	  line indented one level deeper.
1636	- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
1637	  level shallower.
1638	- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
1639	  else that is commented.
1640	
1641	Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
1642	Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
1643	JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
1644	Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.
1645	
1646	**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
1647	`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
1648	`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
1649	file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
1650	`piton compile` gives:
1651	
1652	```ts
1653	import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
1654	import spec from '../spec/app.pi';
1655	
1656	const button = SaveButton;
1657	const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
1658	```
1659	
1660	It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
1661	'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
1662	(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
1663	Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.
1664	
1665	## 15. Working on a specbase
1666	
1667	1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
1668	   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
1669	   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
1670	   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
1671	   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
1672	   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
1673	2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
1674	   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
1675	   follow them only when relevant.
1676	3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
1677	   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
1678	   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
1679	   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
1680	     `lib/` folder;
1681	   - lowerCamelCase property names;
1682	   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
1683	   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
1684	   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
1685	   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
1686	4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
1687	   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
1688	   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
1689	5. **Validate.**
1690	   - Run `piton check`.
1691	   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
1692	     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
1693	     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
1694	     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
1695	   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
1696	   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
1697	   - Run `piton format --check`.
1698	6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
1699	   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
1700	   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
1701	   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
1702	7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
1703	   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
1704	   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
1705	   flag the gap.
1706	
1707	## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec
1708	
1709	Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:
1710	
1711	- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
1712	  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
1713	  `format` with no path or `-`.
1714	
1715	- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
1716	  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
1717	  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.
1718	
1719	Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
1720	surprise you:
1721	
1722	- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
1723	  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
1724	  package.
1725	- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
1726	  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
1727	  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
1728	  the value on the anchor itself.
1729	- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
1730	  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
1731	- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
1732	  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
1733	  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
1734	- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
1735	  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
1736	- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
1737	  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
1738	  adapter `.pi` files.

# Chat Input Scope

## How To Build

A ChatInputScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A ChatInputScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well as snippets of Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegrationScope
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. While the harness is working, the send button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

#### Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInput.md#chat-input-instruction)

#### Send Options

##### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

##### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.

##### Options

The menu's options, in order:

- "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
- "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it
- "Send to task", with a send icon, only while a task is running with a harness that can be fed more, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and its output is shown, the previous tasks not expanded over it; never on the Ask tab, where a question runs on its own. It sends what is typed, and what is attached, to the running task instead of queueing it, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, and clears the input as sending does. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) still queues, as the send button does

#### Editing Queued

Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor), sets aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab, and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text. Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and the send menu isn't offered.
Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it, cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in progress; so does switching projects.

#### Preview

Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with, at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs, attachments, and send button stay as they are.
The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape> goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

#### Tabs

##### Overview

The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using gpui-kit's default tab styling. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text

###### Either

they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next

or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

##### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
In combined mode, with Chain selected, Chain has no line along its bottom, just as the joined Code and Spec beneath it have none. In separate mode, unselected, it has one, like any other unselected

###### Tab

the tab bar's bottom line runs beneath it, the same colour and

thickness, in the same place, as beneath any other unselected tab, at any display scale. This holds at every window size and display scale, in light and dark mode: in combined mode nothing draws a line beneath Chain at all, rather than a line being drawn and then hidden, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.

##### Help

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) says.

##### Session

At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New conversation button. The questions of the Ask tab have a conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so the figure is the Ask tab's conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon, reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation for the selected tab: the tasks' on Code, Chain, and Spec, the questions' on Ask. The next run in that tab, or in any tab sharing its conversation, starts a new one with no context instead of carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back, even once the project is closed and opened again, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.
It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a task on Code, Chain, or Spec, or any question on Ask, without waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts sent meanwhile queue as ever, and the next task to run from the queue, the first in it, starts a new conversation with no context, the ones after it carrying that one on. That holds even when the running task is the first of its conversation and the harness hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't carried on either.
Its tooltip says which conversation it resets: "Start a new conversation for tasks" or "Start a new conversation for questions", adding, while a run in it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left. It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next task, or question, already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.

##### Usage

Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is the cost of this project's runs since it was opened, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when it reports no cost either. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  its cost.
- This project: the same totals for every run in the project since
  it was opened, tasks and questions, and how many runs there were.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs go, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.

##### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

##### Colour

The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope). With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green; neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.
The send button, both its halves, takes the same colour as the selected tab, purple with Chain selected, but at full strength rather than as a tint, so it stands out against the tinted body. Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never staying solid across a faded button.

#### System Prompt

The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system prompt is sent with it, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.

#### Ask

Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already running.
Each question's progress and results are shown in a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope). The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and first line.
However many questions are asked, the stack is only as tall as its rows, up to 240 pixels, the queue's most, and scrolls beyond that with a [ScrollbarScope](../../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope), kept on the newest question, nearest the tabs, as each is asked. Once it holds more than fit, the stack lays out only the rows in view, as a table does, so a long stack costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a short one, and the drawer's bottom follows the stack's top as ever.
Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status and first line, above its full task table, in the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope), which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time: opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

#### Answer Steps

For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer, the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says. A question closed into the previous answers starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list).

#### Previous Answers

Previous answers are a [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope), shown only while the Ask tab is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers", "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded, "Back to the questions". Each previous answer offers Resend, which asks its question again, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Expanded, the row and the list go into the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope), sliding up from on top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

#### Answer Drawer

[AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope)

#### Selecting Answer Text

The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../../ui/components/selection-popover/index.md#selection-popover-scope) with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The popover also closes when the drawer closes.

#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Projects

The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous answers belong to their project, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says: switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The prompt being written, its attachments, the selected tab, and the Slice toggle stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

#### Escape

Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat input. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) brings it back, from anywhere the chat input isn't beneath something else, as the [MainWindowScope](../../application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope) says.

#### Grow To Fit

The text input is a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input-scope) growing to 12 rows at most. Its single row lines up with the send button.

#### Auto Focus

The chat input should be auto-focused.

#### Syntax Highlighting

Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

#### Lsp

[LSP](../../lsp/index.md#lsp)

#### Harness Mentions

```
overview: Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@` offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself. The placeholder mentions both.

```

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope)

##### Escaping

A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes all mean something. The anchor is exported, so that it compiles, and its userPrompt is a multi-line escape block, which Piton keeps exactly as it is: the prompt's lines, each at the block's indentation, fenced by a line of three backslashes, or of one more than any line of the prompt made only of backslashes, so nothing in it closes the block early. The systemPrompt is written the same way.
Each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported, in the userPrompt and then the systemPrompt, is also listed once, in the order they first appear, as an item of the anchor's references property, left out when there are none; a reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. `piton compile` resolves the references. What the harness receives is the prompt as it was saved, line for line, with each reference replaced by what it resolved to: a dollar-brace by its text, and an at-brace by a Markdown link, from the project directory, to the reference document the project's build writes for it, in the reference root of the config's first adapter, such as .claude/reference, named by its dotted path, and going to the heading for the anchor or property it names once the document is built. A prompt saved by an earlier version, as quoted pieces or as prose, still reads back.

##### Auto Imports

The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there, typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out, character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment then never stops the server finding the names that need importing, both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

##### Attached Text

A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText

###### Property

a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the

order they were attached, keyed text1, text2, and so on. Since attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each is written as a multi-line escape block, as the userPrompt is, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no attachedText property.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

##### Sliced

A prompt sent with Slice on is still written as the hidden anchor, which records that it was sliced, and is compiled the same way, so a prompt that fails to compile fails with Slice on too. But what the harness receives is the prompt as it was saved, line for line, with each at-brace reference replaced by the dotted path it names rather than a link, and each dollar-brace by its text, as ever. Then, for each at-brace reference in the userPrompt, once, in the order they first appear, what `piton slice` prints for it, run in the project directory on the source file and dotted path the reference names, under a line reading "Spec slices:". A slice that fails puts why in its place, and the prompt is still sent. Attached text follows the slices, as it follows the prompt. The system prompt is resolved as ever. A queued prompt keeps whether it was sliced, and the preview shows what the harness would receive with the toggle as it is.
Wherever a sliced prompt is shown, in the latest task's header, among the previous tasks and answers, and in the preview, the prompt as typed comes first, with any text attached to it, and the slices are collapsed beneath it into a single row reading "Show 1 spec slice" or "Show N spec slices", muted, beside a right chevron, as a table's collapsed rows are. Clicking it expands the slices in place, and it reads "Hide N spec slices" beside a down chevron; clicking it again collapses them. Each prompt's slices start collapsed, and stay as they were left for as long as the application runs. What the harness receives is unchanged.

# Prompt Modes Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the code and the spec.

### Shape

#### Description

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
- Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
- Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
- Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
- Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple.

#### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Tasks carry on one conversation, one at a time, and queue while the harness is working. Before one is sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says. Once one finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to the [GitPanelScope](../../../ui/components/git-panel/index.md#git-panel-scope).

#### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own, apart from the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

#### Freeform

A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it, no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file. Otherwise it is a task like any other: it queues while the harness is working, carries on the tasks' conversation, heads the message list, is saved in the prompt history, can be cancelled or resent, and adds a commit note once it finishes having changed files. Its header shows the prompt as it was sent, with no hidden anchor named. It is never sent to another mode, alone or in a batch.

#### System Prompts

Each mode but Freeform sends its own system prompt, from the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope). A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.

# Prompt Sending Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

How a prompt gets to the harness, whether written in the chat input or sent on the application's behalf.

### Shape

#### Description

A prompt is sent in one of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), with anything attached to it. Sending is never blocked by the harness working.

#### Tasks

A task, a prompt in Code, Chain, or Spec, is sent straight away while the harness is free. While the harness is working, it waits in the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor)'s queue instead, in the order it was sent, keeping its mode and attachments, until its turn comes.
When a task is actually sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, the task showing "Building" until the build is over; then its hidden anchor is compiled and run. It heads the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) as the latest task, and is saved in the prompt history, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. A prompt that fails to compile or run fails its task, and doesn't stop the queue.

#### Questions

A question, a prompt in Ask, never queues: it runs straight away, even while the harness is working on a task or other questions, joins the questions stacked above the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s tabs, and is saved among the questions asked.

#### Sending To ATask

While a task is running, more can be sent to it, as to a terminal session, from the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s "Send to task", as it says. What is sent is written as a hidden anchor and compiled like any prompt, its references, attachments, and Slice toggle included, so it can reference the spec, but the spec isn't built first, and its systemPrompt isn't sent, since the run already has the one it began with. It goes to the running task's run as a message of its own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and is not a task of its own: it doesn't head the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list), isn't among the previous tasks, and can't be resent. It is shown in the task's output and kept with its record, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says. A message that fails to compile isn't sent, and a notification titled "Could not send to the task" says why, what was typed going back into the input. A message whose task ends before it can be sent is queued instead, as a task, so nothing typed is lost.

#### On The Applications Behalf

Something in the application can send a prompt as if it were written in the chat input and sent from one of its tabs. It goes just the same

##### Way

queued if the harness is busy, shown as a task, and entered in the

history. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone.

#### Resending

A prompt sent before can be sent again, from a Resend button: a small ghost button with a rotating-arrow icon, whose tooltip says it sends the prompt again as it was sent. It sits at the right of the latest task's header, and of the heading of each previous task and previous answer, beside its chevron; clicking it never opens or closes the item.
Resending sends the prompt as it was typed, in the mode it was sent in, with the text that was attached to it, and sliced or not as it was, as though it were sent afresh from the chat input: a task queues while the harness is working, a question runs straight away, and either is compiled anew, against the spec and system prompt as they are now, building the spec first as any task does, and saved in the history as a new task or question. The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone, and so is the Slice toggle.

#### Cancelling

The task under way can be cancelled, from a Cancel button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, whose tooltip says "Cancel this task", at the right of the latest task's header, beside its Resend button, shown only while the task is building, compiling, or running. A task is cancelled straight away, whatever the harness is in the middle of: a build or compile under way is abandoned before the task is run, and a run is stopped, the harness's process ended, not left to finish its turn.
A cancelled task keeps the output it had so far, and its status reads "Cancelled", as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) shows, in the history as much as in its header. It adds no commit note, and any change the harness had already made to files is left as it is. The queue carries on after it, as it does after a task that fails, sending the next prompt waiting in it, and the next task carries on the same conversation. Questions are not cancelled with it.

#### Sending To The Other Mode

A task sent in Code alone can be sent to Spec, and one sent in Spec alone can be sent to Code, from a small ghost button beside its Resend button, tinted the colour of the mode it sends to, whose tooltip says "Send to Spec" or "Send to Code". It sits wherever Resend does for a task, at the right of the latest task's header and of the heading of each previous task, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. Tasks sent in Chain, questions, and prompts whose mode isn't known don't offer it.
Sending to the other mode is resending, as above, in every way but the

##### Mode

the prompt is sent in the other mode, with that mode's system

prompt, and saved in the history as a new task in that mode.

input.message:
The Freeform tab is in, after Ask. It sends the prompt to the harness exactly as typed, plus any attachments, and otherwise behaves like any other task. `cargo build` is clean. In the full suite, 312 pass, 1 is ignored, and every failure is either one of the two you listed or passes when run alone. Nothing is committed, and nothing under spec/, .claude/ or CLAUDE.md was touched.

**One edit to your in-progress work you should check:** `chat_input::tests::usage_summary_opens_its_details` (uncommitted) resizes the window to 640px to test a narrow bar. With a fifth tab, New conversation now spills 19px past the bar at that width. I changed the width to 700px (src/chat_input.rs, near line 2582, with a comment). It means the bar overflows at 640px in the app itself. If that matters, the tabs or controls need to shrink rather than the test changing. The spec doesn't say how narrow the bar must stay usable.

## What changed
**src/chat_input.rs**
- `SendMode::Freeform` (383), with label "Freeform", saved key `freeform`, id `freeform-tab`, and help text "Passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written." (396–444).
- `other()` returns None for Freeform.
- The tabs are now Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, Freeform (`FREEFORM_TAB` 203), all rendered flush (1710). Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab wrap through all five.
- Joining the tabs under Chain now only applies to Code and Spec (it used to be "everything but Ask").
- Colour: a new `Hues` struct (223) adds grey, taken from the theme's tertiary text colour. `tint()` (247) now goes red → purple → blue → green → grey and back to red.
  - `blend()` (337) keeps the coloured side's hue when fading to or from grey, so green→grey and grey→red never pass through another hue.
- Test-only `set_slices` (724).

**src/hidden_anchor.rs**
- `freeform()` (455) builds what the harness gets: the prompt as typed plus the attached text, with no system prompt. Nothing calls piton.
- Old history records still load: the mode is read by key, and records with no mode still come back as no mode.

**src/prompt_mode.rs**
